questions.q: In SARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)12, what is the season length?
questions.why: The last number, m, is the season length: 12.

questions.q: Which statement about AIC is true?
options: Lower is better, and it punishes extra parameters
Higher is better
It measures the test error directly
It can be compared across any two models
why: Correct: AIC = 2k - 2 ln L has a penalty 2k.
Lower is better.
AIC is an in-sample score. It is a guide to the test error, not the test error.
It is only comparable for models fitted on the same data with the same differencing.

questions.q: ln(L) = -150, k = 4 parameters. What is the AIC?
What is the null hypothesis of the Ljung-Box test?
options: The residuals are white noise (no autocorrelation)
The residuals have a unit root
The residuals are normal
The model has no seasonal part
why: Correct: a small p-value means leftover autocorrelation.
That is the ADF null for a series.
Normality is tested by other tests.
The test does not look at the model structure.

questions.q: Your SARIMA has the lowest AIC, but the Ljung-Box p-value is 0.001. What do you do?
options: Treat it as unfinished: look for a missing term (seasonal, AR or MA) and refit
Ship it, AIC is lowest
Increase d to 3
Remove the test
why: Correct: the residuals still hold structure, so the model can improve.
Lowest AIC with bad residuals still leaves structure unmodelled.
Over-differencing would make things worse.
Removing the check hides the problem.

questions.q: Model A is ARIMA(1,0,0) and model B is ARIMA(1,1,0), fitted on the same series. A has AIC 500 and B has AIC 450. Can you say B is better?
options: No, AIC is not comparable across different d
Yes, 450 is lower
Yes, because d = 1 is always better
No, because AIC cannot be used for ARIMA
why: Correct: differencing changes the data (and its length), so the likelihoods are on different data.
The numbers are not on the same data, so the comparison is not valid.
d = 1 is not always better. It depends on the series.
AIC can be used for ARIMA models with the same d.

questions.q: Monthly sales with trend and a yearly season. A baseline seasonal naive has MAE 20. Your SARIMA has MAE 19.5 on the test set but twice the compute cost. What would you say?
options: The gain is small. Check it on more origins and consider if it is worth the cost
Ship SARIMA, it is lower
Use the mean forecast instead
Add more orders until MAE is 15
why: Correct: judge the lift with several backtest origins and weigh it against cost and complexity.
A 2.5% gain on one test may be noise.
The mean ignores trend and season.
Searching more orders until the test MAE drops is overfitting to the test set.
